source.title: Swing-by Dynamics in Concept Learning and Compositional Generalization
source.authors: Yong-Yi Yang; C. Park; E. Lubana; Maya Okawa; Wei Hu; Hidenori Tanaka

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plot labels and figure details are garbled in the web extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It measures test loss over training time in structured identity-mapping and diffusion-model tasks, using OOD compositional generalization rather than the original double-descent settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on OOD test loss over training time, including double-, triple-, and quadruple-descent-like curves. Learning-order and concept-signal results are not rows because they do not measure a claim version. The paper does not sweep model size or training sample count.
record.test_reason: The study reports test loss over training time, on an OOD compositional test point, and finds a fall-rise-fall (and triple/quadruple) shape. That bears on V2 in a new setting: SIM regression and a toy diffusion task. The authors frame Swing-by as a distinct mechanism from in-distribution epoch-wise double descent (footnote 2), so this is a new-setting result, not a T2 replication. No size or sample sweeps are run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors present Swing-by as a novel, distribution-shift mechanism. It produces a double-descent-like curve but they distinguish it from epoch-wise double descent, which is attributed to noise or overparametrization and in-distribution error. Multiple descent needs specific signal strengths and initialization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SIM Gaussian-mixture regression and a synthetic compositional diffusion task, tracking OOD test loss over training time. It does not reproduce the original model-size or sample-size sweeps or test an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The non-monotonic curve is stronger in low-dimensional settings and absent in the reported high-dimensional setting; the paper also reports multiple descents under selected signal strengths and tuned initialization seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: The non-monotonic OOD loss arises from staged growth and suppression of Jacobian entries (Swing-by), with small data variance and no label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Epoch-wise non-monotonic test loss can arise from sequential feature-learning stages under distribution shift, independent of label noise or overparametrization.

record.problems: The reported loss curves are primarily presented in figures without numeric values in the text. Multiple-descent examples are shown for selected parameter settings and tuned random seeds. The results concern OOD compositional loss and do not test model-size or sample-size double descent.

untested.parts: In-distribution test error, label-noise settings and standard deep-network benchmarks. All results concern a single OOD compositional test point or composition.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
Not tested: no capacity sweep past an interpolation point.
Not tested: no recounting of complexity.

missing.what: One-layer linear models give monotonic output trajectories with no Swing-by and no non-monotonic loss. Shown analytically (Theorem 4.1) and in experiments; a no-effect condition for V2.
Truncating the training distribution away from the test point has little impact on the Swing-by dynamics.
Training loss decreases monotonically while the OOD test loss is non-monotonic.

record.verdict_notes: Classified as T3, not T2, because the measure is OOD loss at a single composite test point and the authors explicitly separate the mechanism from classic epoch-wise double descent. The V2 link is borderline; a stricter reading would move these results to fits_no_version. All evidence is figure-only, the multiple-descent examples use tuned seeds, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve over model size.
Tests OOD compositional test loss, not whether the same curve holds for ordinary in-distribution test error across the original settings.
No variation in training-sample count near an interpolation threshold.
Does not sweep model capacity across an interpolation point or test a general capacity-risk curve.
Does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

Tests whether multiple descent-like phases can occur in specified toy-network settings. It does not establish that label noise or variance drives the peak, or test whether optimally tuned regularization removes it; the reported σ values describe data variance/diversity, not label noise.
Does not recount complexity by an effective parameter number or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
